# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where the commit finishes it;
  the `task-lifecycle` check reads it off the branch.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

`.github/workflows/` is the one directory a converge cannot push to, so both files here drifted from what their packs now seed. This is the PR that carries them.

**The dashboard Pages workflow** was still the pre-`gh-pages` shape: it built the site itself, from `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/build-site.mjs`, a path the pack moved to `tooling/` in 60902.15. Every run since dies with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, so the last green deploy is from 2026-09-14 09:49 and the live page is a tree built by the in-workflow build — which reads no `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_*` repository variables, which is why the page offers a pasted-token box. Replaced with the pack's own stub: `workflow_dispatch` only, a `gh-pages` checkout and the four Pages actions. This unblocks #422, whose `gh-pages` push already landed as `ee1f8c7`.

**The executor** is `converge-workflows.mjs`' own output, clearing a standing world-scope advisory: `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` — what `deploy-oauth-exchange` needs to put the sign-in endpoint live — were never named statically, so they never reached the job. `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` goes, named by no declared task since the dashboard retired `fleet-digest`, and the legacy `task:ready` trigger with it.

`check_the_world.mjs` is clean on this branch; it reported the executor advisory before.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/ClaudiniteCanary/.claude/skills/writing-handover-issues

# Writing a task for a human

An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
almost always written like the first.

The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
thread, and does three of six steps.

## The body has exactly two parts, in this order

1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
the same screen twice.

That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.

543:#### Turning sign-in on
544-
545-Copy this into the deployment's own issue, substituting its owner and repo — it is the
546-checklist the adoption handover points at. Notes are below it, deliberately: a reader
547-working through these has the settings page open in the next tab.
548-
549-- [ ] Register a GitHub App — `https://github.com/settings/apps/new`
550-- [ ] Set its **Homepage URL** and **Redirect URI** to `https://<owner>.github.io/`, and tick **Enable wildcard matching** beneath the redirect URI
551-- [ ] Tick *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation*
552-- [ ] Untick **Webhook → Active**
553-- [ ] Under **Permissions → Repository**, set Contents, Issues, Metadata and Actions to **Read-only**, then press **Create GitHub App**
554-- [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — the App's General page, under the app name; begins `Iv23`
555-- [ ] Add it as the variable `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID` — `<repo>/settings/variables/actions/new`
556-- [ ] Press **Generate a new client secret**, and copy the value under **Client secrets** — shown once
557-- [ ] Add it as the Actions secret `DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` — `<repo>/settings/secrets/actions/new`
558-- [ ] Install the App on the account holding the repos — `https://github.com/settings/apps/<app-slug>/installations`
559-- [ ] Copy your Cloudflare **Account ID** — `https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/workers`, the right-hand sidebar under *Account details*; 32 hex characters
560-- [ ] Add it as the variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` — `<repo>/settings/variables/actions/new`
561-- [ ] Create a Cloudflare API token — `https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens` — template **Edit Cloudflare Workers**, name `claudinite-dashboard-deploy`, **Account Resources** *Include* the hosting account, **Zone Resources** *Include · All zones*
562-- [ ] Copy the token — shown once, on the confirmation screen
563-- [ ] Add it as the Actions secret `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` — `<repo>/settings/secrets/actions/new`
564-- [ ] Run `create-work-item claudinite-dashboard/deploy-oauth-exchange`, and copy the `workers.dev` URL it reports
565-- [ ] Add it as the variable `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL` — `<repo>/settings/variables/actions/new`
566-
567-**Done when** a signed-in viewer's rate pill reads `…/5000 · user`.
568-
569-Notes. **Webhook → Active** arrives ticked and the form then refuses to submit without a
570-Webhook URL; this App is a sign-in credential and receives nothing, so unticking it is
571-what lets the registration through. The token's **Zone Resources** are asked for because
572-the template carries a zone-scoped permission, and *All zones* is the answer that always
573-works: this deploy never exercises them, calling only `/accounts/<id>/workers/…`.
574-Installing the App lands you on the redirect URI,
575-and `https://<owner>.github.io/` is a **404** unless that owner happens to keep a
576-user-site repo — expected, and not a failed step: the root is registered so that wildcard
577-matching permits the project pages beneath it, and sign-in returns to the dashboard's own
578-URL rather than to the root. The two Cloudflare credentials are the
579-[deploy task](tasks/deploy-oauth-exchange/README.md)'s, which says why the API token is
580-that narrow. The App is installed per *account*, not per repo — a user token reaches only what
581-it is installed on, so an uninstalled account renders every member row as *not visible to
582-you*. Wildcard matching on the `github.io` root covers every project Pages site on that
583-host, so one App serves every dashboard you own. The sign-in pair are repository
584-variables rather than config or secrets: they are what you set while standing in the
585-App's settings, the exchange URL is minted by the deploy rather than authored, and
586-neither is confidential — the client id is in every authorize URL and the exchange URL is
587-fetched by the browser. The client id alone does nothing; the pair is what makes the
588-button appear.
589-
590-### Why "just use my existing GitHub login" is not on that list
591-
592-It cannot be. A browser will not send github.com's session cookies to
593-`api.github.com`, and the API does not accept cookie auth cross-origin at all —
594-"already logged in to GitHub" is not a credential a web page can spend. Every
595-GitHub-backed dashboard you have used either asked for a token or ran an OAuth
596-sign-in; there is no third option.
597-
598-Sign-in is the closest thing, and it is genuinely *your* permissions: after one
599-authorization, every call runs as you. The only piece that cannot live in the page
600-is the `code` → token exchange, which needs the app's client secret **and** hits an
601-endpoint that sends no CORS headers. That is what `exchangeUrl` points at —
602-[`oauth-exchange.mjs`](tooling/oauth-exchange.mjs) is a deployable
603-implementation. It sees one code, returns one token, and never touches repo data.
604-
605-## Caching
606-
607-A fleet view is only affordable because most of what it reads does not change.
608-Three strategies, because the data has three shapes — see
609-[`cache.mjs`](src/read/cache.mjs):
610-
611-| Data | Strategy | Why |
612-|---|---|---|
613-| Repo content (task declarations, the tree) | keyed by **commit SHA**, never expires | a path at a sha cannot change, so an unmoved `main` costs zero calls |

input.title: claudinite-dashboard: the setup steps only a human can do
input.body:
Adopting `claudinite-dashboard` (#154) brings the steps no Action can perform. This deployment is Canary's own page, and the App that signs the fleet dashboard in already covers it, so what is left is copying that App's two public values onto this repo.

- [x] Enable GitHub Pages with source **GitHub Actions** — [Pages](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/settings/pages)
- [ ] Copy `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID` — [Claudinite's variables](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/settings/variables/actions), the value begins `Iv23`
- [ ] Add it here under the same name — [new variable](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/settings/variables/actions/new)
- [ ] Copy `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL` — [Claudinite's variables](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/settings/variables/actions), a `workers.dev` URL
- [ ] Add it here under the same name — [new variable](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/settings/variables/actions/new)

**Done when** loading https://missingbulb.github.io/ClaudiniteCanary/packs/claudinite-dashboard/ signed out shows **Sign in with GitHub**, and clicking it returns you signed in with the rate pill reading `…/5000 · user`.

## Why

Pages is ticked: the workflow has deployed successfully here, most recently [run 34829965495](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/actions/runs/34829965495).

The two variables are what make the Sign in button appear; neither is confidential — the client id is in every authorize URL the page builds and the exchange URL is fetched by the browser, which is why they are variables rather than secrets. Until they are set, a viewer reads GitHub anonymously at 60 requests/hour per IP, and the page offers a pasted-token box instead.

Nothing has to be registered or deployed for this repo. The App's redirect URI is `https://missingbulb.github.io/` with wildcard matching, which covers every project Pages site on that host, and the exchange endpoint's allowed origin is that same host — so one App and one endpoint serve every dashboard on this account. That is also why there is no Cloudflare step here: `deploy-oauth-exchange` mints an endpoint, and one already exists.

The Sign in button will only reach the page once #429 lands — the deploy workflow frozen here still builds the site itself and never reads these variables (#428).

### Removed: the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` step

This issue used to ask for a fine-grained PAT covering all repositories. It is not needed and has been dropped. It existed for the `fleet-digest` task, which the dashboard pack retired in 60827.2 along with that handover step; nothing in this repo declares the secret, and this deployment is a repo dashboard covering no other repo in any case. The executor's wiring drops it in #429.

{"number":1983,"title":"Dashboard: require sign-in on its own screen, remember the credential, and put account controls under the avatar","body":"## The problem

The dashboard asks for a sign-in every day. The credential lives in `sessionStorage`
(`packs/claudinite-dashboard/auth.mjs`), which dies with the tab, and nothing ever re-signs
automatically — so a daily viewer presses **Sign in with GitHub** every morning. GitHub remembers
the authorization, so the click buys nothing; it is pure friction.

Two things came out of looking at it:

- **The credential's lifetime is the viewer's call, and the page never asks.** `sessionStorage` is
  the right default on a shared machine and the wrong one on a personal laptop. The module's own
  comment records the omission as deliberate, on the grounds that the page is not entitled to make
  that decision — which is the argument for *asking*, not for deciding the strict way.
- **The main screens carry sign-in state they should not have to.** The fleet and repo views can
  render anonymously, half-signed-in, or with a pasted token, and every one of those states has to
  be handled in the chrome beside the data.

## The change

1. **Remember me.** A checkbox beside each sign-in. Unticked, nothing moves: `sessionStorage`, dies
   with the tab. Ticked, the credential goes to `localStorage` and survives a browser restart until
   sign-out. Toggling after signing in moves the credential the viewer already has, rather than
   applying only to the next sign-in.
2. **Sign-in is a gate, on its own screen.** No view of the dashboard without a credential. The
   fleet and repo views stop rendering any sign-in affordance at all; the credential explanation
   moves off the topbar explainer and onto that screen. The pasted-token path stays, on the same
   screen, as the fallback for a deployment with no OAuth pair configured and for local development.
   A `?repo=owner/name` deep link survives the gate.
3. **The topbar reduces to what you are looking at.** Everything belonging to the viewer rather than
   the view — the login name, the rate budget, **Reload**, **Clear cache**, **Sign out**, and the
   "How this reads your repo" note — moves into a menu behind the signed-in avatar. The title reads
   **Claudinite Fleet Status**.
4. **Clear cache must not sign the viewer out.** `cache.mjs` claims the whole `claudinite-dashboard:`
   prefix in `localStorage`; a remembered credential sits under that prefix, so the purge sweep and
   the quota-eviction sweep would both reach it — the latter first, since a raw token is not JSON
   and sorts as undecodable. The cache's ownership narrows to its own versioned prefix.

## Verification

`test/auth.test.mjs` and `test/cache.test.mjs` cover the storage behaviour: the default still dies
with the tab, a remembered credential survives a simulated restart, un-ticking demotes the existing
credential, sign-out leaves no copy in either store, a browser that refuses storage still signs in
for the tab, and neither cache sweep can reach the credential. The three cache tests fail against
the unfixed `cache.mjs`.

The chrome itself was driven in Chromium against the pack's own dev server: the gate signed out, the
token fallback with no OAuth configured, and the account menu open on the fleet view.

input.title: Dashboard: retire the pasted-token credential, so sign-in is the only way in
input.body:
## The problem

#1983 built the sign-in gate and deliberately kept the pasted-token path beside it: "the fallback for a deployment with no OAuth pair configured and for local development". Standing on the canary's page, that fallback is what a viewer actually meets:

> https://missingbulb.github.io/ClaudiniteCanary/packs/claudinite-dashboard/ — *This deployment has no sign-in configured, so it reads with a token you …*

The owner's call is that this mode should not exist. A viewer who lands on a dashboard is told to go and mint a PAT, which is worse than the thing sign-in was built to replace, and it is the state every deployment reaches by default — the two variables that light the button are unset until someone sets them, so "no sign-in configured" is not an edge case, it is the shipping default.

It also costs the pack a second credential path to hold correct everywhere: two providers in `auth.mjs`, two branches of the gate in `app.mjs`, `credentialAdvice`'s two-way split, and the remember-me pair documented for both.

## The change

Sign-in is the only route to a credential. The token provider goes, and with it the paste box, the `signin-how` fork, and the two-provider branch in `credentialAdvice`.

What that leaves to decide, and what this issue has to answer rather than assume:

- **A deployment with no client id / exchange URL.** It cannot sign anybody in, so the gate has nothing to offer. It should say that plainly — this dashboard is not finished being set up, here is what its owner has to do — rather than offering a worse credential. Naming the two variables on that screen turns the state into a one-line instruction for the person who can fix it.
- **Local development.** `tooling/serve.mjs` is the path the fallback was really kept for. It needs its own answer — a dev-only credential the served page accepts, not a production affordance every viewer sees.

## Where it is

`packs/claudinite-dashboard/src/read/auth.mjs` (the two providers and the `token` half of the storage pair), `src/app.mjs` around lines 127–139 and 223 and 296, the gate markup in `src/index.html`, and the README's "Turning sign-in on" notes which currently present the box as a supported choice. `pack.mjs`'s `adoptionHandover` still frames the sign-in step as a decision — "leave it on the pasted-token box, or …" — and becomes an instruction.

Found from the canary: missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary#153.

input.title: Dashboard: the account menu is a paragraph with buttons above it, where it should read like GitHub's
input.body:
## The problem

The menu #1983 put behind the avatar opens as: a login and **Sign out** on one row, **Reload** and **Clear cache** on the next, the rate pill, and then a six-line paragraph explaining the cache strategy — SHA keying, ETags and `304`s, the 24-hour and six-hour TTLs, budget pressure, what **Clear cache** does, and the `?repo=owner/name` parameter.

The paragraph is the menu. It is four times the height of everything above it, it is open every time the avatar is clicked, and it is read once ever — a viewer opening this menu is going for **Sign out** or **Reload**, and on every one of those visits the explanation is in the way. The markup's own comment argues the credential explanation belongs on the gate "rather than in the account menu, where it would be re-read by everyone who went looking for Reload". That argument applies to this paragraph too; it just was not applied.

Compare GitHub's own avatar menu, which is the thing a viewer's hand already knows: a header with the account, then flat rows of one icon and one label each, grouped into sections by hairline rules, **Sign out** last. No prose anywhere. Everything in it is a destination or an action.

## The change

Style the menu after that: the account header, then rows rather than clustered buttons, sections separated by rules, sign-out last, and the rate pill as a row of its own rather than a floating chip.

The caching explanation stops being always-on. It is reference material, so it belongs behind a disclosure in the menu's last section — one row that opens it — or on the gate beside the credential explanation, which is the screen where a viewer is already reading about how the page works. Either answer is better than the current one; the issue is which, and that is worth deciding once rather than per-element.

## Where it is

`packs/claudinite-dashboard/src/index.html` — the `details.setup#account` block and the `.account-head` / `.account-actions` / `#account .pill` rules under "the account menu".

Raised by the owner against the live page, with GitHub's menu as the reference.

input.title: A pack that reshapes a seeded workflow strands every member already carrying the old one, silently
input.body:
## What happened

The canary's dashboard has been failing to deploy since 2026-09-14, and nothing said so anywhere a person or a check would look.

`claudinite-dashboard` seeds `.github/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml` once, at adoption. Since then the stub has been reshaped twice — 60830.1 added the two `vars` lines, 60902.15 moved the build out of the workflow into `publish-pages` and shrank the stub to a `gh-pages` checkout and the four Pages actions. Both rows say an existing member needs the stub re-seeded. Nothing makes that happen, and nothing notices that it has not.

So the canary kept running the adoption-era copy, which still does

```
node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/build-site.mjs
```

— a path the pack moved to `tooling/`. Every run since dies with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` ([run 34952297234](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/actions/runs/34952297234)). The `publish-pages` task pushed its build to `gh-pages` as designed and then parked on the deploy's failure, which reads as the task being broken. The page meanwhile went on serving the last tree the old in-workflow build produced — a build that reads no repository variables, so the deployment's sign-in could never have appeared however its variables were set. Three visible faults, one frozen file.

`.github/workflows/` being unconvergeable is settled (#797, #649). What is missing is the signal: the member cannot be *fixed* automatically, but it can certainly be *told*.

## The change

An advisory in the world sweep, shaped like `executor-workflow-secrets` (#1796), which is the same problem already solved once for one file: a declaring pack's `seedOps` name a template and a destination, so a check can compare the member's copy against the template it was seeded from and report a stale one, with the re-seed as its fix line. That covers every pack's seeded file rather than the dashboard's, and it runs where the executor advisory already runs.

Exact-match is too strict — a member is entitled to edit its own copy — so the comparison needs a rule. Options worth weighing in the issue: compare against the template the member's *stamped* pack version shipped (drift then means "the pack moved, you did not"), or have `seedOps` carry a marker line the check reads, the way the executor's `# claudinite:secrets` marker bounds the region a converge owns.

Whatever the rule, the point is that the member gets told once, in the sweep, with the fix line — rather than the fleet discovering it a broken deployment at a time.

## Evidence

missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary#428 and its fix missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary#429, which also had to carry the executor converge for the same reason — `converge-workflows.mjs` had two secrets to add that no push could deliver. Both files in one member were stale at once, which is a reasonable prior for the rest of the fleet.

content.text:
Done. Here's what happened.

**Root cause behind items 1–3 was mostly one file.** `.github/workflows/` is the one directory a converge can't push to, so both of Canary's workflow files were frozen at adoption while their packs moved on.

```
.github/workflows/
  claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml — replaced with the pack's current stub:
      workflow_dispatch + a gh-pages checkout + the four Pages actions.
      The frozen copy still built the site itself, from a path the pack
      moved to tooling/, so every deploy since 09-14 died MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
  claudinite-executor.yml — converge-workflows.mjs' own output: adds
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET (what
      deploy-oauth-exchange needs and never received), drops
      FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN and the legacy task:ready trigger.
```

**Fixed on Canary**

- [#428](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/428) / [#429](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/pull/429) — the two workflow files. `check_the_world.mjs` is clean on the branch; it reported the executor advisory before.
- [#153](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/153) — the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` box is gone. It was for `fleet-digest`, which the dashboard pack retired in 60827.2 along with that very handover step; no task here declares it. Pages is ticked (it has deployed successfully). What's left is two repository variables copied off the Claudinite repo — this account's App already covers `missingbulb.github.io` by wildcard, so nothing needs registering or deploying for Canary.
- [#422](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/422) — the `Internal Server Error` was GitHub's and the push did land later (`ee1f8c7`). A retry now would just park on the frozen workflow, so it's held until #429 merges rather than re-queued.

**Filed on Claudinite**

- [#2069](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2069) — retire the pasted-token credential; sign-in the only way in. Names the two things it has to answer: what an unconfigured deployment's gate says instead, and what `serve.mjs` uses locally.
- [#2070](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2070) — the account menu, styled after GitHub's, with the caching paragraph behind a disclosure instead of open on every visit.
- [#2071](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2071) — the canon gap under all of this: a pack reshaping a seeded workflow leaves every existing member broken with no signal. Proposes the world advisory shaped like `executor-workflow-secrets`.

One thing I did not do: set Canary's two `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_*` variables — I have no tool that writes repository variables, so they stay as the checklist in #153.

> ⚠️ Still open: [#429](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/pull/429) needs your merge before the dashboard deploys again or the Sign in button can reach the page; the two variables in [#153](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/153) are yours to paste.

**The README badge row** goes entirely. It had dangled at `tidy-repo`, a blocking `reference-integrity` finding, which is #362's finding for the second time — `barriers` was the first. ```
README.md — the generated pack-badge row, removed entirely
```

It dangled at `tidy-repo` (declared nowhere, not in the mount). That's [#362](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/362)'s finding for the second time — `barriers` was the first, patched in September by deleting the one entry. Claudinite retired the mechanism that writes the row in [Claudinite#1750](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1750): members keep theirs only because nothing takes it away, and an unmaintained row dangles again at whichever pack is dropped next. So I removed the block rather than the entry — a recurring blocking finding is exactly the noise the canary's own rules say destroys its signal. No new canon issue: #1750 already decided this, the canary just hadn't followed through.

Both sweeps are clean on the branch. [#429](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/pull/429) now carries three commits and closes #428 and #362.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- canary-role: What ClaudiniteCanary is for and how to work in it — the live canary for Claudinite's consumer-safety gate. Use before changing anything in this repo, and when a canary rehearsal comes back red and you have to decide what the red means.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own — research it against the vendor's live documentation, capture what is portable as a technology skill with declared checks, and wire the project's use of it as a task in its structural local pack. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, get the owner's approval of the plan itself — a line per step, the dependency graph, each link's automerge policy — before filing any of its issues, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/ClaudiniteCanary/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it
   again. (1)
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)
